#1013. Tenerife player Jesus de Miguel dies in hospital after on-pitch collision

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The striker died as a result of injuries sustained in an incident during Tenerife’s second-tier match on Monday

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel has died aged 30 from injuries sustained in an on-pitch collision during a match on Monday.

De Miguel was initially treated on the pitch after he suffered a cardiac arrest following a clash late in added time with Andorra ​goalkeeper ⁠Jesus Owono, before being rushed to hospital. The match was abandoned following the collision.

Tenerife initially reported that he was “stable, despite the severity of his condition” in the intensive care unit of Hospital Universitario de Nuestra Señora de Candelaria in Santa Cruz, before reporting that his neurological condition had worsened in the early hours of Tuesday.

The Spanish second division club released a statement saying he had passed away at 8am on Tuesday. It said: “Heartbroken, with a lump in our throats and unable to believe this is true, we at CD Tenerife announce the tragic passing of Jesus de Miguel Alameda.

“There are no words of comfort. There is absolutely nothing that can ease this overwhelming sense of sadness.

“We stand with his devastated family, with his loved ones, and with the entire Tenerife footballing community, who today mourn this cruel turn of events.

The Spanish Football Federation announced the postponed of Tuesday’s Copa del Rey and Copa del Reina matches. “We extend our deepest condolences to his family, friends and loved ones, as well as to Club Deportivo Tenerife and all its fans, whom we accompany in these moments of great sorrow,” it said.

The Spanish Footballers’ Association also expressed its “deep sorrow” at his death, writing: “His loss leaves a huge void among those of us who shared his passion for football, his commitment to the football community, and his work in defense of the rights of fellow professionals.

“The Board of Directors, all the workers of AFE and the footballers’ collective wish to convey our deepest condolences to his family, friends and loved ones, as well as to his teammates at Club Deportivo Tenerife.

“In these moments of immense sadness, we send you all our love, support and solidarity. You will always be part of our family. Rest in peace, comrade.”

A statement from Andorra read: “With broken hearts, we want to send our most sincere condolences to the family of Jesus de Miguel, to all his teammates, friends, and to CD Tenerife. Rest in peace.”

The scoreline was 2-2 when De Miguel was sent through on goal, with keeper Owono rushing out and colliding with him in the chest. Owono, who was shown a straight red card for the challenge, immediately ran to his side as De Miguel appeared motionless, along with other players from both teams and medical staff, before the 30-year-old was taken to hospital.

De Miguel, who made his professional debut in 2015 for Leganes B, signed a three-year contract with Tenerife in 2025 and helped the club earn promotion back to the Segunda Division, scoring 11 goals in 29 games.

Several Spanish teams, including Barcelona and Real Madrid, paid tribute, while Fifpro, the world players’ union, said: “Fifpro is deeply saddened by the passing of CD Tenerife player Jesus de Miguel. Our thoughts are with Jesus’ family, friends, team-mates, everyone at CD Tenerife, and all those affected. Rest in peace, Jesus.”

La Liga president Javier Tebas expressed his shock and said the league would work to support the club and De Miguel’s family, and said he would speak to Tenerife about potentially postponing their next match out of concern for the players’ welfare. Speaking in an interview with Television Canaria, Tebas also raised the possibility of a joint tribute between La Liga and the Segunda Division.

Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin said: “We are heartbroken by the death of Jesus de Miguel Alameda. We have searched for words and found only silence. In that silence, our hearts and thoughts are with his family, his team-mates, everyone at Tenerife, and all those who mourn this tragic loss.”

All Uefa matches this week will be preceded with a moment of silence in memory of De Miguel.

Manchester City have been given a lifeline to sell an underperforming player, after defeat against Brighton & Hove Albion made it three losses in four.

The Citizens started their campaign with seven straight wins in the Premier League under new manager Enzo Maresca, but the last two weeks have brought Manchester City back down to earth, with champions Arsenal replacing them at the top of the league over the weekend.

Despite heavy investment over the summer, there are several questions over Maresca's best XI – and now, City could be offered an option to offload one of their bigger signings in the coming months.

Over the past three seasons, City have invested over a billion pounds in their playing squad, buying the likes of Ayyoub Bouaddi, Enzo Fernandez and Elliot Anderson over the summer transfer window of 2026, for a combined £300 million.

Despite the Premier League's charges hanging over the club, it's business as usual for the transfer team – but now, one of the club's biggest-ever signings could be offered an exit route after a disappointing start to his City career.

According to Fichajes and Bernabeu Digital, Real Madrid still have an interest in Enzo Fernandez – despite the Argentine becoming City's all-time record signing over the summer for a fee worth around £125m.

Los Blancos are monitoring City's charges, and although they're linked with Alexis Mac Allister of Liverpool, historic interest in his Argentina colleague hasn't died down.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Fernandez was a nine-figure move for Chelsea in January 2023 after his breakout performances for Argentina at the 2022 World Cup, finding some of his best form under Maresca: but despite City buying both Anderson and Bouaddi over the summer – and having the likes of Rayan Cherki and Phil Foden as options at No.10 – City smashed their transfer record for the star to reunite the two Enzos in another blockbuster transfer.

The midfielder hasn't set the world alight so far at the Etihad Stadium, however, with Erling Haaland visibly frustrated with his team-mate on Saturday after he failed to win a single duel in the defeat to Brighton.

Fernandez ranks in the 66th percentile for duel-winning this season, as per Gradient Sports – and when Anderson plays alongside the 25-year-old in a double-pivot, the England international is left with much of the dirty work.

While FourFourTwo understands that City are committed to Fernandez and wouldn't have broken their transfer record for the Argentine unless they were convinced of his abilities, Fernandez's role at the club is closely linked to manager Enzo Maresca's.

Should City suffer this season and Maresca leave the club, that would place Fernandez's future on shakier ground – and with a wealth of options in City's midfield, it's not inconceivable that City would listen to offers for the star next summer: whether they have been relegated from the Premier League or not.

Fernandez is worth €120m, according to Transfermarkt. Manchester City travel to RB Leipzig as Champions League action continues this week.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Arsenal full-back Riccardo Calafiori could leave the club in a shock move.

That's according to a new report, which claims that the champions have to be wary that their superstar Italian could be about to depart North London after three years.

Calafiori has been excellent for Arsenal this season – but with the star's contract reaching the two-year mark next summer, the Gunners might have to consider cashing in if they can't extend.

The Gunners won their first fixture at Anfield in 14 years yesterday, with Calafiori a member of the back four that kept yet another clean sheet in the Premier League to go top of the table.

The 24-year-old has arguably been the North Londoners' player of the season thus far, chipping in with goals and assists in attack, while remaining a part of the most impressive back four on the continent.

This has alerted Real Madrid, who are weighing up a move for the defender, as per TEAMtalk.

Los Blancos signed Marc Cucurella over the summer to bolster their options at left-back, but with Calafiori able to play centrally, Bernabeu boss Jose Mourinho is said to value the Arsenal man's versatility, considering him a “dream” signing and Real “enquiring” about a move, after playing the star nine times during his time as Roma manager.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

FourFourTwo understands that Real were in the race for the Italian when he eventually left Bologna for North London in 2024, with Arsenal rushing to complete the signing, believing that it was a significant upgrade in that area of the pitch.

But while Calafiori has unlocked a new dimension to manager Mikel Arteta's attack when he's been fit, his contract ticking down – with an expiry in 2029 – may represent an opportunity to sell the star.

FourFourTwo understands that the champions plan to address his extension along with the likes of Martin Odegaard, Jurrien Timber and Declan Rice, though with Calafiori having suffered a number of injuries during his time in English football, Arsenal may have to weigh up whether an attractive bid – and Calafiori's own interest in Real – makes a sale appealing.

Calafiori suffered a potentially career-ending knee injury as a teenager, only to bounce back impressively and rebuild his career via a spell in Switzerland.

Since moving to the Premier League, however, the Rome-born star has suffered eight separate injuries, missing 13 matches in all competitions after Christmas last season, and seeing Piero Hincapie start the Champions League final ahead of him.

Calafiori is worth €65 million, according to Transfermarkt. Arsenal travel to Slavia Prague this week as Champions League action continues this week.

Under-fire Manchester United boss Michael Carrick has made a remarkably candid admission regarding his Old Trafford future

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Carrick appears to have accepted that his tenure at Old Trafford could soon be brought to an abrupt end.

Speaking ahead of Man United’s next game, a Champions League showdown with AS Roma, Carrick was fatalistic in tone when questioned about the mounting speculation surrounding his position.

Rather than offering standard managerial press conference fare of defiance in the face of public scrutiny, the 45-year-old openly acknowledged the reality of his situation.

"I can’t look into the future, I don’t know what’s gonna happen,” Carrick admitted, in quotes via The Athletic. “I am really looking forward to the game tomorrow, you might think I’m crazy with the results we’ve had. Whatever happens will happen after that, whatever direction it goes in.”

The mood around the club has turned following a run of just two wins in nine matches across all competitions. A five-game winless streak, an early Carabao Cup exit, and a return of seven points from their opening nine Premier League fixtures has left Man United drastically off the pace.

Recent domestic displays, which include failing to capitalise against 10 men versus Manchester City and Tottenham Hotspur, were compounded by a dispiriting Champions League defeat away to Atletico Madrid, after which Lisandro Martinez spoke out against the club hierarchy.

Martinez broke rank to deliver a stinging critique of the club's summer recruitment, reportedly sparking an argument with a teammate on the flight back to Manchester. With a dressing room unravelling and Carrick's gentler approach failing to provoke a response, the popular view is that the club's faith in his faculties to turn things around has plummeted.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

To some, his latest quotes indicate a recognition that the writing is on the wall, and with the November international break coming up, that could be the opportune time for the club to sever ties with the former interim head coach.

Old Trafford is likely to have a new first-team manager before long - national outlets have already linked Brighton’s Fabian Hurzeler alongside more experienced coaches Antonio Conte and Unai Emery.

At a club the size of Manchester United, once a manager hums 'que sera, sera', the inevitable is rarely far behind.

#1008. Germany news: Emergency at Leipzig airport sparked by novice driver

Two men breached a fence at the Leipzig/Halle airport while practicing for a driving test. Meanwhile, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz announced an industrial AI partnership with Nvidia. DW has more.

This blog is now closed. Below is a roundup of the stories from and about Germany on Monday, October 19, 2026.

Berlin's Left Party, the Greens and the Social Democrats are set to move ahead on talks to form the next coalition government in the capital city.

The SPD's state leadership approved the motion with a wide majority in an online session, and the Greens voted overwhelmingly in favor of talks at a small party convention.

The Left Party has not scheduled a conference until October 31 because members of the party may be away because of school holidays.

The Left Party is hoping to have Elif Eralp lead the state government.

The coalition talks are set to open after weeks of tense negotiations and a dispute over alleged antisemitism within the ranks of the Left Party.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang unveiled a new artificial intelligence (AI) cooperation at a glitzy investment summit in Berlin on Monday evening.

"Germany is open for business," said Merz at the Invest in Germany event, adding that the combination of German engineering and cutting-edge AI technology would help strengthen the country's economy in the long term.

"Germany is open for investment and Germany is ready to grow at a faster pace," the chancellor continued, before joking: "If I were Jensen Huang, I would put on my leather jacket, take a flight to Berlin, meet the German Chancellor, and tell him, 'I'm ready to invest.'"

The partnership with Nvidia is intended to speed up the digital transformation of German industry and secure the country's technological sovereignty.

According to the company, Nvidia invested nearly $1 billion in Germany last year and holds stakes in numerous start-ups and established companies.

But Europe's largest economy has nevertheless struggled to attract foreign investment after years of weak growth, with high energy prices and labor costs continuing to deter businesses.

German officials were hoping that Monday's summit, which was attended by more than 200 domestic and international investment executives, would showcase Germany as an attractive investment destination, highlighting its sound public finances, status as the only G7 country with a triple-A credit rating, its universities, skilled workforce and tariff-free trade within the EU single market.

Further behind-closed-door talks are set to take place on Tuesday.

Do you remember those arrests in Germany last week, connected to an arson attempt at a Starlink control center in Poland?

The government in Warsaw called it a hybrid attack and accused Russia of recruiting organized crime elements for the alleged crime.

It's much too early to say for sure, but Bulgaria has now issued a pair of European arrest warrants against German citizens in a case that seems rather reminiscent in several regards.

The two 19-year-olds are accused of driving in from Serbia claiming to be tourists, setting fire to a series of antennae south of Sofia, and leaving the country again within a matter of hours.

Hermann Höllenreiner, a Sinti German raised in Bavaria who survived the Nazis' Auschwitz concentration camp as a child, has died aged 92.

Munich's Hanser Verlag publisher and the International Auschwitz Committee said that he had passed away last Friday, October 16, in Mettenheim in Bavaria, surrounded by his family.

Höllenreiner, known as "Mano" to his large Bavarian Sinti family, spent time at the Auschwitz-Birkenau, Ravensbrück and Sachsenhausen camps as a child.

"Only later in his life did he start to tell his story and became a major witness of the era, who hauntingly reported on the horrors of Auschwitz, the perpetrators and the victims, and above all of the still-persistnent discrimination of Sinti and Roma in Europe," Christioph Heubner, executive vice president of the International Auschwitz Committee, said.

"Mano Höllenreiner's biography and tales of suffering were enough for more than one life. What he saw with his own eyes as a child in Auschwitz and what was done to him — for many decades he didn't know how to speak out about it," Heubner said, thanking Höllenreiner for his "courage and humanity" in ultimately telling his story.

Höllenriener managed to flee one of the so-called "death marches" fleeing extermination camps in as Allied armies approached.

Author Anja Tuckermann told his story in a book whose title roughly translates as: "Mano. The boy who didn't know where he was."

He was initially found on a roadside and rescued by liberated French prisoners, who took him home with them. In 1946, he was reunited with surviving relatives in Germany.

Two men have admitted to breaking through a fence at Leipzig/Halle airport while one of them was practicing for a driving test, an incident that triggered a major security operation, police said on Monday.

The two, aged 20 and 32, handed themselves in to the police on Sunday evening, following the incident. The broken fence was first discovered by airport staff late on Saturday.

Police said the 20-year-old had been at the wheel despite not having a valid license.

An investigation was opened into the learner driver for fleeing the scene after breaking through the fence.

The mass-circulation Bild newspaper reported that the car involved, of which fragments were found at the site, was an Audi.

The airport was the site of a security scare in August, when an explosives-laden drone was found there near Ukrainian cargo planes.

German officials accused Russia of having planned an attack, something Moscow denied.

Germany's Rheinmetall defense group on Monday announced that it had acquired Romania's Mangalia shipyard at auction in partnership with Swiss shipping giant MSC.

Rheinmetall said it had paid approximately €138 million ($154 million) for the facility.   Acquisition is expected to be finalized within a few weeks.   Rheinmetall and MSC plan to develop the Black Sea shipyard near Constanța into a dual-use site for civilian and military shipbuilding for both domestic and international markets.

Rheinmetall says its Naval Systems division will use the facility to build four vessels commissioned by the Romanian government, including two 96-meter (305 foot) offshore patrol vessels and two 43-meter diving support vessels.   The company also intends to modernize the shipyard's infrastructure and expand its capacity.

"In doing so," said the company, ​"Rheinmetall ⁠is creating a scalable foundation for future ⁠projects in ​southeastern Europe and strengthens its position in a strategically important market."

The Foreign Ministry has summoned Iran's ambassador after two men were convicted of preparing attacks on Jewish figures and pro-Israel targets in Germany at the behest of Tehran.

"We vehemently condemn Iran's activities. We will not allow Iran to threaten our liberal society," the ministry wrote on X.

"We do not tolerate attacks on Jewish life and those who defend it anywhere, and particularly not in Germany," it wrote.

A Hamburg court on Thursday sentenced a 54-year-old man and a 43-year old man respectively to 8 1/2 and 4 1/2 years in prison for having spied on the president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, Josef Schuster, and Volker Beck, the president of the German-Israeli Society (DIG).

In the court's opinion, their actions were carried out in preparation for terrorist attacks, including the planned murders of  Schuster and Beck.

The court said the 54-year-old, who was said to have also done the groundwork for an arson attack on a kosher food store in Berlin, received his orders directly from officers in the Quds Force.

The Quds Force is the branch of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) that is in charge of extraterritorial operations.

German industrial businesses employed some 496,000 fewer people at the end of 2025 compared to the start of 2019, according to a survey conducted by the Ifo Institute economic think tank.

Worst-hit has been the automotive industry, a key sector of the German economy, where 123,500 jobs were cut both at carmakers and suppliers, a decline of 13%.

But the metals sector also saw a marked decline in the number of jobs available, dropping 115,600 workers in the period, while the machinery sector bled 64,500 positions.

At the same time, more than 2.2 million additional jobs were created in the service sector, according to Ifo.

It said 391,000 new jobs had been established in the health sector and another 357,000 in social services, including care homes.

Joachim Ragnitz, managing director at Ifo Dresden, said the figures showed an "accelerated structural shift" in Germany.

"Ironically, the very sectors that have sustained our prosperity up to now are shrinking," he said.

"The new jobs are for the most part not being created where Germany is especially productive and innovative. That may slow down our growth potential in the future."

A German woman has died in a climbing accident in the Italian Alps, mountain rescuers said on Monday.

The 32-year-old woman, who was an experienced mountaineer, fell more than 50 meters (164 feet) to her death while on the Cengia dei Camosci, a difficult route on the 2,323-meter Grande Nabois mountain near the Slovenian border.

The rescue service said the accident was caused when a climbing hold gave way under the woman, who was accompanied by an Austrian fellow climber at the time.

Investigations are underway to clarify the exact circumstances of her death.

Carmaker Volkswagen intends to freeze the salaries of some 660,000 employees worldwide until 2030 as the company, along with the entire car industry, faces a range of challenges that have impacted its profits.

Trade union IG Metall confirmed earlier media reports of the plans, citing information given to employees by the works council.

The works council described the plans as unrealistic and said there would be considerable resistance to them.

If the company does implement them, employees could lose an estimated 10% of their purchasing power by the end of the decade.

The news comes after VW decided in September to cut 50,000 jobs worldwide in the coming years in addition to the reduction of 50,000 positions that had already been agreed.

Four plants in Germany are also at risk of being closed between 2031 and 2034.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Less than a third of leadership positions in Germany are held by women, a lower level than the EU average, statistics released on Monday showed.

According to the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), citing figures from the EU statistics authority Eurostat, women held just 30.3% of leadership positions in Germany, compared with 35.9% in the whole of the EU.

Only Cyprus, Italy and the Netherlands have lower rates than Germany in the bloc, while Sweden has the highest, at 44.4%, followed by Latvia, Estonia and Poland.

"The low proportion of women in leadership positions in Germany is particularly striking, as almost as many women as men are employed here," Destatis said, comparing the situation with Italy, which has almost the same level of female leadership but a much lower rate of female employment overall.

Destatis defines leadership positions as those involving the management of small companies, the management of large companies or departments within them and high administrative posts.

A two-day conference entitled "Invest in Germany Summit" is to begin on Monday evening in Berlin as the government seeks to shore up public-sector spending with private money.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz will deliver the opening speech at the conference, which will be attended by an expected 200 representatives from large German and international companies.

The CEO of the US chip manufacturer Nvidia, Jensen Huang, is to be one of the key guests at the conference.

The German government is looking to cooperate strongly with the company, whose products are central to the boom in artificial intelligence, in a bid to help Germany catch up in the sector.

The German Economic Institute (IW) has, however, warned against any too high expectations from the summit, saying that high costs for labor, energy and bureaucracy in Germany were a deterrent to investment in the country.

"It would be naive to believe that the summit will change that in the short term. Companies don't choose Germany because of a promotional event. What matters is whether they can make money here," IW director Michael Hüther told the DPA news agency.

He said it would be more effective if the government were to swiftly implement its reform agenda.

A study by Allianz Research has shown that investment in Germany fell by 6.4% between 2019 and 2025, while it grew by 6.7% in the rest of the eurozone and a whole 20.2% in the US.

The DW newsroom in Bonn bids guten Tag to all its faithful readers at the start of a new week!

Today, we will be looking at a conference in Berlin that will seek to attract private investment in Germany to help make the country fit for the future, with the field of artificial intelligence a key focus.

New statistics are also to be released on Monday on women in leadership and government positions in Germany and the EU in 2025.

And the Leipzig/Halle airport has resumed normal operations after a security incident involving a breached fence triggered a large-scale police operation.

This occurred just weeks after an explosives-laden drone that German officials believe was intended to carry out an attack on behalf of Russia was found at the airport.

Read on for more on these and other stories connected with all things German.

This kind of nonsense usually only surfaces around the international break.

An incredible stat, however, has re-emerged concerning Manchester City goalkeeper Ronald Waterreus (remember him?) and his opposite number Nick Colgan (remember him? No?) from around 20 years ago that's sure to blow your mind.

And after digging, it gets even stranger.

Back in 2004/05, only two matches across the entirety of Great Britain in all competitions ended 7-1 – which is not that strange, given that it's an unusual scoreline.

The first came when Man City smashed Barnsley in the League Cup in September, with Waterreus between the sticks for the Citizens and Colgan conceding those seven goals for the Tykes.

The other match that ended with that scoreline, you ask? Well, obviously it was another League Cup game – this time north of the border – between Rangers and Dundee United.

The goalkeepers in that match, you ask? Take a wild guess.

That's right: David James' back-up, Waterreus, had moved to the Gers in search of more game time in January, while Colgan joined United on loan in January 2005.

But the oddness doesn't end there: both matches were club debuts for Waterreus.

The symmetry is startling, especially when you consider that the Dutchman played just a handful of times at City, while Colgan made just two appearances during that stint in Scottish football.

With the fact making its way back onto social media recently, it's probably time to remind everyone of just how much of an incredible coincidence it really is.

William Saliba has been pictured back training with Arsenal’s first-team in a huge boost to Mikel Arteta’s side.

#1005. Spurs win three in row for first time in 616 days to pile pressure on Sage

For the first time in 616 days, Tottenham Hotspur have won three Premier League matches in a row. Three different managers have been sacked in that time, and the mood in north London had plunged to grim lows, but finally there is a sense that something truly exciting is stirring at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.

This victory over Crystal Palace was not as impressive as last week’s triumph at Chelsea, but it did not need to be. After Palace striker Jean-Philippe Mateta was sent off in the 13th minute, Spurs simply had to make their numerical advantage count. They did so with relative ease, taking complete control of possession and creating endless goalscoring opportunities.

Roberto De Zerbi’s team ended the night with 34 shots to Palace’s two and with 758 completed passes to Palace’s 149. The goals ultimately came from two defenders, Archie Gray and Jan Paul van Hecke, but there was a long list of Spurs players who might have scored here.

Spurs take the lead through an Archie Gray header! ⚪ https://t.co/qSCECkOJur

Did this defeat mark the end for Pierre Sage, the Palace manager? The Frenchman was only appointed in June but it has been a grisly start to the campaign. Palace have the worst defence in the league, have lost six of nine games and have not produced any truly encouraging performances in the Premier League.

Even in the two games Palace have won, against Fulham and Nottingham Forest, they were lucky to do so. The likes of Sean Dyche and Thomas Frank, both of whom would be strong candidates to replace Sage if Palace do pull the trigger, will no doubt have been keeping an eye on events here.

“I am really aware of the situation,” Sage said. “I don’t like this situation. [But] you can trust in me, I will never give up. I want to be the first on the pitch on Monday. I have the rage to train more. It’s not me to decide this thing [his future]. If I have one hour, I will give my best for one hour. If I have 10 years, I will give my best for 10 years.”

The decision for Palace chairman Steve Parish, then, is whether this result represented a continuation of the team’s problems or was an aberration caused by the early red card. It would be reasonable for Sage to claim this match was out of his hands from the moment Mateta lunged at Spurs captain Micky van de Ven, but such an argument might not carry much weight with Palace sitting 18th in the table.

The challenge was foolish in the extreme by Mateta, a player who was much more successful in exiting this game than he has been in his numerous attempts to leave Palace in recent transfer windows. At first glance it did not seem the worst tackle, but the replays were damning: Mateta led with his studs and made forceful contact with Van de Ven’s ankle.

It was an inexcusably brainless act, after just 13 minutes of play, and the same could be said of Palace’s defending from a right-wing corner a few minutes later. Mohammed Kudus swirled the delivery to the back post, where Gray was unmarked. Yes, Palace were defending with 10. But no, that does not justify the inability of Sage’s players to spot Gray. Even more embarrassingly, the Tottenham player was unmarked again from another corner shortly afterwards.

It was not the first time this season that Palace’s cause has been undermined by a red card. When they lost at home to Ipswich Town in September, Axel Disasi was sent off after 34 minutes. An absence of discipline? Perhaps. Sage might argue, though, that he is not responsible for his players demonstrating a lack of basic brainpower.

Jean-Philippe Mateta receives his first red card for Crystal Palace! 🟥 https://t.co/U9UYb29mbk

All of this was welcomed heartily by the Spurs fans, who celebrated Mateta’s dismissal as though it was a goal. Recent results have restored some of the enthusiasm in this corner of north London and the mood here was buoyant, even before Gray’s opener.

“Now we are playing as a team,” De Zerbi said. “Before the international break, we were playing as many good players but not as a team. We showed our maturity. We are improving.”

The second goal was always coming and it arrived in the 73rd minute, when Van Hecke attacked a wonderful cross by Mateus Fernandes. Palace goalkeeper Dean Henderson saved the first attempt but the ball dropped onto the head of Van Hecke, now seated in the six-yard box, and he happily nodded it home.

Jan Paul van Hecke doubles Spurs' lead! 👊 https://t.co/1Odkkr8wBJ

The new signings at Spurs endured a difficult first few weeks but there were more signs here that they are adjusting to De Zerbi’s system. Sandro Tonali was exceptional in midfield and teenage talent Luca Williams-Barnett also sparkled off the bench. “Tonali was unbelievable,” De Zerbi said. “We played with two players more: Tonali was double.”

Spurs face Leeds United, Ipswich Town, Sunderland and Fulham in their next four league games. The momentum could, and perhaps should, continue to build. Their optimism here contrasted sharply with the angst of Palace, and with the troubled look that was etched on Sage’s face.

“Very pleased for the performance, very tough game. You don’t know 11 [against 11] would be different game but Crystal Palace are very tough because they defend with a low block, no space and we showed we are a mature team. Maybe we could score more goals with more nastiness, but I am very happy because we created many chances. We need more goals for sure. It’s not enough, but we are improving a lot.

“I was very nervous before the game, during the game, after the red card, it’s always better playing with one player more. But today, against this team, they played with this behaviour, all behind the line of the ball, aggressive. Very tough game.”

When asked if Spurs are looking up the table, he replied: “We don’t forget the ambitions. We have to look behind what was the situation two weeks ago. In the last two years, two times 17th in the table, many games without a win in front of our fans. We have to stay focused. They are improving, increasing the level of performance.”

Speaking to Sky Sports, the Palace defender said: “Definitely was frustrating. It was one of the first tackles of the game. And we felt like we were doing well and it is unfortunate. We go again.

“The main message was don’t concede again, stay tight as a defence and try to hit them on the counter. That is the best plan when you’re down a man.

“Unfortunately, it didn’t happen today. We know what we can do as a team, as a back five, the whole unit. There were some positives in the games, but I can’t say much when you lose. We just have to go again.

“Hopefully, the next game we win. The main message is to stay together as a team. We know what we are capable of. It is staying confident and bouncing back.”

We have to analyse to improve the results but to improve the results we have to improve all aspects.”

Pierre Sage, the Palace manager, lightened the load after knocking Fulham out of the Carabao Cup in midweek but seemed surprised that the fans have remained so supportive. “It’s always a good sign,” he said. “I appreciate it [singing his name at Craven Cottage] very much and I can thank them but I prefer they are with the team than me alone. Because I’m the manager, but I’m not the most important part of the team, of the performance and the result. I think the players need it more than me but it’s really appreciated from me.”

Asked what he has learnt about fan sentiment from looking at social media, he said: “I think they understood what happened, why we are not perfect at the moment. We don’t care who is the most responsible for the situation. I take the responsibility. I have no problem with that. I just want people to understand what we do and why.”

Two changes from the starting line-up that took on Newcastle: captain Dean Henderson is back in goal and Oscar Mingueza replaces Anan Khalaili at right wing-back.

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of this Premier League encounter between Tottenham and Crystal Palace.

Last weekend, Spurs enjoyed a historic result, beating Chelsea 2-0 at Stamford Bridge for only the second time in the league for 36 years thanks to Mike Penders’ own goal and Mathys Tel’s stunning solo strike. Consistent team selection and simpler patterns should be the order of the day at Stamford Bridge this season, but Alonso doesn't seem to be offering that yet

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The billions spent on young players and the constant churn for accountancy tricks, the erratic form and the bottom-half finishes: Chelsea are engulfed in an identity crisis of their own making and everybody knows Xabi Alonso needs a transitional year to sort this mess out.

What’s needed is stability, order, calm; qualities Chelsea’s owners carelessly abandoned across the first four years of their tech bro, move-fast-and-break-things philosophy. The decision to hire Alonso as ‘manager’ and not ‘head coach’ - and to allow over-30s into the training ground - tells us they have learnt their lesson.

But does Alonso, rocking up in this new and better environment, appreciate the chaos that came before him, that still hums in the background at Stamford Bridge? Judging by the instability, disorder, and erratic tactical setups this season, the answer is no. Alonso is a world-class coach, but he appears to be overthinking his tactics, which is the last thing such a tangled-up squad needs.

In nine Premier League matches, Alonso has used six different combinations in defence and five different combinations of a two-man midfield. As we have highlighted before, he made the strange decision to trial a Henderson-Barco pivot in the defeat at Brentford, and then he got found out by an even stranger strikerless 4-4-2 in the 2-0 defeat to Tottenham.

On Saturday, the tactical overthinking was a little harder to spot, but, again, complexity was unnecessarily introduced to a fixture against a Manchester United team waiting to be beaten. Chelsea were a shambles in the first half thanks to a strange use of Cole Palmer that scrambled brains in the middle of the park. When Alonso corrected his error with a far more normal 4-2-3-1 in the second half, Chelsea strode to victory.

In that chaotic end-to-end first half, Chelsea consistently lost possession in the middle of the park (leading to quick United transitions, then quick Chelsea counters back the other way, hence the carnage) because Palmer’s position meant the passing lanes weren’t open. Chelsea, lacking depth (or ‘verticality’), could not pass forward in an orderly fashion and therefore could not maintain a solid shape:

In the second half, Alonso normalised things by playing Palmer higher and suddenly Manchester United couldn’t cope with the passes through the lines.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Even the crucial opener was indirectly affected by this, with Manchester United players seemingly distracted away from Morgan Rogers by Palmer’s lurking presence.

There is a clear lesson here for Alonso: his players – young, new to the club, recovering from the tornado that was 2025/26 – need a firm hand on the tiller; consistent team selection, simple patterns, and the opportunity to discover what it means to play for a normal club.

In other words, these players have spent enough time charging around in circles. They need to be taught how to walk before they can run.

Alex Keble is a freelance football journalist based in London, specialising in tactical analysis. He has written for BBC Sport, Goal, The Mirror, The Independent, Football 365, and many others. As well as covering Premier League football, Alex works as a child therapist.

Police in Spain have confirmed they have opened a “routine” investigation into possible involuntary manslaughter following the death of Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel, who died in hospital on Tuesday after suffering a cardiac arrest as a result of a collision during a match on Monday.

De Miguel, 30, collapsed on the pitch after a clash with Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono, who had rushed out of his area to clear the ball but struck the forward in the chest. The match was then abandoned and Owono was shown a red card following the incident, which took place in stoppage time of the second division fixture.

De Miguel was taken to hospital after receiving treatment on the pitch. Tenerife initially reported that he was “stable, despite the severity of his condition” before reporting that his neurological condition had worsened in the early hours of Tuesday. They confirmed his death at around 8am on Tuesday.

While Spain’s National Police said prosecutors would be involved, authorities in the Canary Islands said the opening of an investigation into the footballer’s death was a routine procedure. Under Spanish law, any death that is deemed non-natural automatically triggers a judicial inquiry.

In a statement, Tenerife said: “Heartbroken, with a lump in our throats and unable to believe this is true, we at CD Tenerife announce the tragic passing of Jesus de Miguel Alameda. There are no words of comfort. There is absolutely nothing that can ease this overwhelming sense of sadness.”

Owono, a Equatorial Guinea international, has deactivated his Instagram account since the incident. A statement from Andorra read: “With broken hearts, we want to send our most sincere condolences to the family of Jesus de Miguel, to all his teammates, friends, and to CD Tenerife. Rest in peace.”

Several Spanish teams, including Barcelona and Real Madrid, paid tribute, while Fifpro, the world players’ union, said: “Fifpro is deeply saddened by the passing of CD Tenerife player Jesus de Miguel. Our thoughts are with Jesus’ family, friends, team-mates, everyone at CD Tenerife, and all those affected. Rest in peace, Jesus.”

La Liga president Javier Tebas expressed his shock and said the league would work to support the club and De Miguel’s family, and said he would speak to Tenerife about potentially postponing their next match out of concern for the players’ welfare. Speaking in an interview with Television Canaria, Tebas also raised the possibility of a joint tribute between La Liga and the Segunda Division.

Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin said: “We are heartbroken by the death of Jesus de Miguel Alameda. We have searched for words and found only silence. In that silence, our hearts and thoughts are with his family, his team-mates, everyone at Tenerife, and all those who mourn this tragic loss.”

All Uefa matches this week will be preceded with a moment of silence in memory of De Miguel while the Spanish Football Federation announced the postponed of Tuesday’s Copa del Rey and Copa del Reina matches. “We extend our deepest condolences to his family, friends and loved ones, as well as to Club Deportivo Tenerife and all its fans, whom we accompany in these moments of great sorrow,” it said.

Dwarf reed snakes start their speedy getaways by surging forward and throwing their bodies over their heads, similar to the movement of a human front flip. (Yosuke Kojima, Ibuki Fukuyama)

In times of trouble, dwarf reed snakes (Pseudorabdion longiceps) can use a cartwheel-like motion to quickly get away. Researchers found that the animals can control the movement by keeping their heads at roughly the same level and pointing in the same direction. This rolling enables the snakes to move around four times faster than they can by slithering. It’s unusual for a snake to move in such a conspicuous way, experts say. But “it’s nice to be surprised by weird snake behaviour occasionally”, says herpetologist Frank Burbrink.

The New York Times | 3 min read (free registration required)

The number of conference papers retracted by the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers on 23 October — the largest bulk retraction by a scholarly publisher ever. (Nature | 3 min read)

The mechanical strain placed on the skeleton during physical activity might prompt bones to release proteins that slow ageing, a study in mice suggests. Researchers found that gently squeezing the legs of mice to simulate the movement of exercise triggered force-sensing cells called osteocytes to secrete molecules that rejuvenate immune cells and reprogram cells in other organs to a younger state. Mice that went through this faux exercise regime lived around three months longer on average than did mice that didn’t.

Since 2016, a layer of water in the Antarctic that has a major influence on Earth’s oceans has changed, with unknown consequences for the world’s climate. With less melting sea ice to feed it each year, the Antarctic Intermediate Water (AAIW) has rapidly become saltier and denser, and sits slightly deeper in the ocean — which might change the way surface water circulates into deeper layers. “The Antarctic region is the freshwater engine of oceans around the globe,” says fluid dynamicist and study co-author Bishakhdatta Gayen.

The deadly avalanche and flood that swept through Nepal’s Rasuwa district in August is an urgent wake-up call, argues a group of mountain-hazard experts. “The unprecedented scale of the damage shows that current approaches of assessing and managing these risks have failed,” they say. “Moreover, with global warming accelerating, further disasters of this magnitude are expected.” (Nature | 14 min read)

Dangerous diseases can present with new symptoms as they evolve, thwarting the systems that have been put in place to detect epidemics. “Unless clinicians recognize that unusual symptoms warrant investigation, even the most advanced tracking systems cannot keep up,” argue infectious-diseases specialist Serge Tonen-Wolyec and virologist Laurent Bélec. They outline a ‘symptom preparedness’ approach that, for example, helps clinicians to act on the intuition that they are dealing with something unusual.

Metascientist Jen Gold, co-founder of the UK government’s metascience unit, shares her advice on how to build such a unit — which studies how research is funded, performed and evaluated — so it can add value to national funding bodies. Working in small teams is essential, because it forces efficient time management, she says. The data infrastructure to share the unit’s results with external researchers is another must. “The barriers to improving science funding are often organizational,” Gold writes. The success of other governmental metascience units will “depend on getting those factors right”.

In his new book The Ends of Race, humanities scholar Geoffrey Galt Harpham chronicles how people attempted to use science to justify racism in the nineteenth century — and the scientific pushback. “Ultimately, the discrediting of the concept of biological race emerged as a triumph of scientific self-correction,” writes journalist David Silverberg in his review.

Physician Ellen Ellis reflects on spending 378 days in a 158-square-metre habitat alongside three others, growing crops, navigating communication delays and conducting suited outings on a simulated Martian surface. (Reuters | 7 min read)

#999. Bigger but not better: Why UEFA have killed the early stages of the Champions League

Join The Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation plus sign you up to our newsletter.

League phase games may be entertaining, but that does not matter without jeopardy

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In April 2021, European football faced an existential threat. Twelve of the continent’s biggest clubs announced a plan to break away from the Champions League and form a European Super League, a closed-shop competition designed to guarantee them regular games against each other.

The dirty dozen would not have to qualify and could never be relegated, an affront to the traditions of European football and the principles of sporting fairness. The backlash was swift and fierce, and within days the project was dead in the water.

The Champions League survived, but only after a fundamental overhaul that gave the drivers of the Super League project much of what they wanted. Plans to switch from the old 32-team group stage to a 36-team, Swiss-style league phase had already been cooked up before the Super League news broke, yet the reforms reflected a desire to keep the elite clubs happy. We are now in the third season of this format, enough time to conclude that UEFA’s flagship tournament has been made worse by its introduction.

That is not to say the old group stage was perfect. After 30 years, it had grown stale and predictable. Dead rubbers were common, as dominant teams regularly wrapped up qualification early. Surprise early exits became increasingly rare. The tournament only came to life in the knockout rounds.

Yet the league phase has solved hardly any of those issues while creating new ones of its own. No fewer than 144 matches are required to eliminate just 12 teams, most of whom were expected to bow out early anyway.

The league phase forgives more than a priest in Las Vegas. It is possible to lose five out of eight games, as Benfica did last term, and still reach the knockouts. In 2024/25, PSG won only one of their first five outings yet ended up finishing 15th, before going on to lift the trophy. The margin for error is considerable.

The league phase creates an illusion of direct comparison. In most domestic leagues, you play every team twice. In the Champions League, you are ranked alongside sides who have played entirely different opponents. Some clubs have much tougher fixture lists than others, yet this is not (and cannot be) reflected in the standings.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

In theory, there are fewer dead rubbers than before. A top-24 finish is all that is needed to extend your participation beyond the league phase, but there are advantages to ending the campaign as high up the table as possible. The top eight progress directly to the round of 16, while teams finishing between ninth and 16th earn home advantage in the second leg of their knockout phase play-off. Yet the reward for finishing in the top eight - the chance to skip a round - is an odd one. UEFA's biggest incentive to excel in its tournament is to play less of it.

The principal reason the league phase was brought in was to offer more blockbuster clashes early on, which were relatively rare in the old system of eight groups of four. This season we have already seen such titanic tussles as Real Madrid vs Inter, Atletico Madrid vs Manchester United, Manchester City vs PSG, PSG vs Barcelona and Bayern Munich vs Arsenal.

At first glance, these fixtures would appear to have delivered the goods. PSG beat both Manchester City and Barcelona 4-2 in pulsating affairs. Bayern and Arsenal drew 2-2 in a game full of quality at the Allianz Arena. There were chances galore in Real Madrid’s 2-1 victory over Inter on matchday one.

UEFA's biggest incentive to excel in its tournament is to play less of it.

Yet for all the entertainment on show, these encounters were much less gripping than comparable contests in the knockout stage. The football was technically impressive, but the lack of jeopardy left many feeling numb. Significance had been stripped away. Without the feeling that it really means something, a meeting of European heavyweights feels like little more than an exhibition game.

The problem is, both UEFA and the continent’s elite clubs will be happy with the new arrangement. More games means more money for everyone involved. And while there is a risk of losing a couple of matches when you have to play the likes of Real Madrid or Bayern Munich, it is unlikely to put qualification at risk. After all, you can amass enough points to advance by beating Sabah, Viking and Slovan Bratislava.

The Champions League knockout stage remains the pinnacle of the club game. Memorable ties become iconic in a way that is impossible in the league phase. The Champions League will be appointment viewing again once we reach the round of 16. Until then, Europe’s biggest tournament feels strangely inconsequential.

Greg Lea is a freelance football journalist who's filled in wherever FourFourTwo needs him since 2014. He became a Crystal Palace fan after watching a 1-0 loss to Port Vale in 1998, and once got on the scoresheet in a primary school game against Wilfried Zaha's Whitehorse Manor (an own goal in an 8-0 defeat).

#998. Lionesses discover Nations League opponents as Sarina Wiegman's side eye LA Olympics qualification

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

England missed out on the 2024 Paris Olympics in agonising fashion

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Sarina Wiegman's England will face France, Austria and Portugal in the UEFA Women's Nations League, a competition that doubles as qualifying for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics.

The draw also placed the Republic of Ireland, Wales and Scotland in League A.

Only the team finishing top of each group secures a place at the Games, with group winners also advancing to the Nations League semi-finals.

The Republic of Ireland have the hardest-looking assignment on paper, having been drawn alongside world champions Spain, as well as Norway and Switzerland.

Wales must contend with Denmark, Italy and Iceland, while Scotland's group features Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden.

Northern Ireland, competing in Group B, will meet Poland, Finland and Belarus.

Matchdays one and two are set for February and March, with the third and fourth rounds of games following in April. The final league stage fixtures come in June, ahead of the Women's World Cup in Brazil.

The semi-finals are due to be played in October, while the third place play-off and the final are scheduled for late November and early December.

Teams finishing fourth in League A will drop into League B, while the winners of League B will move up.

England missed out on the Paris Olympics in 2024 and representing Team GB after failing to win their Nations League group the previous year.

The Lionesses were placed in a group alongside the Netherlands, Scotland and Belgium. Despite winning 6-0 in their final group game against Scotland, England were still pipped to top spot by the Netherlands on goal difference.

Wiegman’s team will not want to slip-up again, but will not have things all their own way in a group that also contains France.

England have also not secured their spot at next year’s World Cup yet, as they must first get past Ukraine in a two-legged play-off, with the two games taking place later this month and in early December.

England have achieved significant success under Wiegman in recent years, winning the Euros in 2022 and 2025, either side of making the World Cup final in 2023.

They will now set their sights on qualifying for next year’s World Cup ahead of a push for Olympic glory the following year.

#997. Bulgaria seeks suspects in Germany after Starlink sabotage

A Bulgarian court has issued arrest warrants for two young German nationals suspected of setting fire to Starlink antennas. The case is reminiscent of another in Poland, which Warsaw says was orchestrated by Russia.

Bulgaria on Monday issued European arrest warrants against two 19-year-old German nationals, saying it suspected their involvement in the sabotage of a series of Starlink antennas near the capital Sofia.

"The evidence gathered makes it possible to conclude that there are reasonable grounds to suspect the involvement of the two defendants," the court in Sofia rules, granting a request from prosecutors.

Ukraine's military uses Starlink's military-grade satellite internet service Starshield for battlefield communications amid Russia's invasion.

Bulgaria does not directly border Ukraine, but it is on the Black Sea, one of the flashpoints of the conflict. A similar case in Poland, which does directly border Ukraine, led to a total of four arrests last week, also in Germany.

The two teenage suspects are accused of deliberately setting fire to the antennas on the evening of October 9.

Of 18 in a mountainous region south of Sofia, three were destroyed entirely, two were partially burned and three more were damaged, according to prosecutors.

Prosecutors say the suspects entered from Serbia in a car with German license plates, claiming to be tourists, staying just a few hours around the time of the alleged crime.

Plamen Tonchev, the head of Bulgaria's domestic intelligence agency DANS, said he was working on the assumption that it was deliberate sabotage and said other such acts could not be ruled out in future.

News of the arrests follow just a week after a total of four people were arrested in Germany, accused of sabotaging a Starlink satellite communications station in central Poland in late September.

German police detained three resident men and a woman, two of them Turkish nationals, early last week.

Polish officials said they believed that Russia was behind the sabotage attempt, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk calling it an act of "hybrid warfare."

The domestic intelligence agency also claimed that Russia had cooperated with organized crime elements in Germany on the alleged operation.

Meanwhile, in the Baltic, Lithuania's prime minister on Sunday said that Russia was likely behind an attempted arson attack on a company hosting communication hardware for Starlink satellites.

#996. Suzuki howler costs Aston Villa crucial points

Aston Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki went from being serenaded with a chorus of “world’s No 1” to making a bizarre blunder that denied Unai Emery’s side a third successive Premier League victory.

The Villa manager, however, preferred to focus on a string of important saves from Suzuki rather than the uncharacteristic mistake that allowed Fulham to collect a deserved point.

It all went wrong for the hosts just after the hour mark in a match where Fulham provided more than a few scares before finding the net in unexpected fashion.

Alex Iwobi, who had been denied superbly by a Suzuki save just moments earlier, swung in a corner. It was right on top of the Villa goalkeeper, who tried to keep it out but only succeeded in fumbling it over the line. A frantic attempt to gather the ball was in vain and goal-line technology confirmed the goal stood.

Zion Suzuki drops Alex Iwobi's corner and Fulham are level! 🫨 https://t.co/KwLFMRpKqk

Suzuki appeared to have been put off by the presence of Fulham’s Shea Charles, but Emery refused to single out the player for criticism.

“I prefer to speak about the saves that he made,” the Villa manager said. “This is part of football. I think he played fantastically and he is doing a lot of saves so he can make one mistake. It is part of football. We can be mature about this.

“I still want to see consistency. Over the last five Premier League matches, we are winning three and drawing two. It’s not bad but with our poor start it’s not enough.

“We have to change our mind quickly for Tuesday against Barcelona. We want to test ourselves at this level.”

Villa go to the Nou Camp with a 100 per cent Champions League record to their name this season. But they will need to improve on Saturday evening’s performance to get a result in Spain.

As well as Suzuki’s error, a 14th-minute penalty miss from John McGinn also proved costly.

It was awarded after Leon Goretzka, making his full league debut for Villa, saw his header hit Sander Berge’s raised hand. Nobody appealed at the time but referee Sam Barrott was sent to the touchline monitor by VAR to review the incident and gave the spot-kick.

McGinn’s attempt, however, hit the crossbar and the chance to take an early lead went begging. The Villa captain seemed a strange choice to take the spot-kick as he has only ever scored one career penalty, but Emery defended the choice, saying: “We analysed the penalty takers in the squad and it was McGinn here.”

Penalty MISSED! John McGinn hits the bar 💥 https://t.co/2kBYkYA2BY

Nicolas Jackson was on hand to ease Villa’s nerves before the break, though. the Villa manager had said before the game that the striker’s goalscoring capability meant he was capable of matching the likes of Harry Kane. His assessment was backed up by Jackson scoring the opening goal, after 40 minutes, which summed up the striker in one moment of pure power combined with agility.

Collecting Johan Manzambi’s superbly weighted pass, Jackson forced his way past two defenders before sliding in the goal that put Villa ahead.

Emery’s touchline celebrations said it all as the Senegal forward continues to flourish under the man who knew how to get the best out of him at Villarreal.

Nicolas Jackson scores his fifth league goal in five games! 🔥 https://t.co/W0xmFtW1Gt

Suzuki has also flourished under Emery and he kept Villa in the game with some superb saves.

Robinson put in another cross and Suzuki got a touch that was enough to make Garcia put his shot wide. Villa were living dangerously and the Japanese goalkeeper made another outstanding stop to keep out Iwobi’s header. But then it all went wrong for Suzuki when he fumbled Iwobi’s corner.

That allowed Fulham’s recent revival under manager, Alvaro Arbeloa, to continue – they now have seven points from their past three games.

“We spoke at half-time about what we had to do,” Arbeloa said. “If you want to win a game you have to fight and I think we have to believe in our way, we’ve shown we can beat anyone in the way that we play but we have to be aggressive.

“We created so many chances and at the end it’s one point in a difficult stadium. I’m so happy with the second half because of the way we played, this is the team that we want to be.”

Zion Suzuki had big gloves to fill this summer after the sale of Emiliano Martínez but already appears one of the Premier League signings of the summer.

Aston Villa’s new No 1 epitomises the vibrant energy of Unai Emery’s revamped squad and is a goalkeeper perfectly suited to the modern game.

The Japanese international is Villa’s own version of former Manchester City goalkeeper Ederson, who revolutionised English football with a vast range of passing from his own penalty area.

Of all the daft statements to have come out of Aston Villa – and I am including Doug Ellis’s frequent claims that he invented the bicycle kick – it is hard to think of anything as absurd as suing a pundit for speaking the truth.

Jamie Carragher’s common-sense declaration that Villa manager Unai Emery might consider a move to Manchester United – because it is a bigger club – has apparently inflicted such a deep wound to the self-esteem of Nassef Sawiris, the chairman, that he has initiated a legal complaint.

Sawiris’s short statement, which he published on social media on Friday night, consisted of 37 ill-chosen words. It started by accusing Carragher of “unacceptable insults to the club and its fans”, then concluded with the vainglorious declaration that “Aston Villa will not allow anyone to stop our ascension in English and European football”.

ASTON VILLA XI TO FACE FULHAM: Suzuki, Cash, Lindelof, Torres, Maatsen, Kamara, Goretzka, Alysson, Manzambi, McGinn, Jackson

Subs: Bizot, Harwood-Bellis, Mings, Barkley, Buendia, Garnacho, Mbaye, Joao Gomes, Madjo

Aston Villa manager, Unai Emery, is giving a full Premier League debut to Germany midfielder Leon Goretzka against Fulham this evening.

The 31-year-old joined Villa on a free transfer in the summer, but a knee injury prevented him from making an appearance off the bench until this month’s Champions League tie against Fenerbahce.

Asked what role Goretzka would have with Villa, Emery deadpanned: “The first one is to be available to play.”

Emery had also made a cryptic remark about Nicolas Jackson and Johann Manzambi in his Friday press conference. The suggestion was that they had been merely rested for Wednesday’s Carabao Cup defeat at Bournemouth.

But the Spaniard said: “For different reasons, not only rest.”

Whatever he meant is unclear, but both start for Villa tonight.

Fulham have won their last two league games – against Hull and Coventry.

Manager, Alvaro Arbeloa, has made one change with Sander Berge replacing Hugo Larsson in midfield.

Villa are aiming to win three successive league games for the first time in this calendar year. The omens are good as they’ve beaten Fulham in their last seven league meetings at Villa Park.

Tonight sees a battle between two Spaniards at Villa Park as Aston Villa host Fulham. Both sides are looking to bounce back from disappointing midweeks having been knocked out of the League Cup; Aston Villa lost 3-0 at Bournemouth, while Fulham fell to a 1-0 defeat at home against Crystal Palace.

After a slow start to the season in the league, Aston Villa’s form has picked up, which includes handing Manchester City their first defeat of the season a week ago. After this evening, Aston Villa have games against Barcelona and Manchester United before the international break but Unai Emery has insisted his full focus is on this game.

“If we are thinking after the match against Fulham, then we are making a mistake and we are completely wrong,” Emery said. “We are prioritising the Premier League, and this is the message. To keep our consistency and demands means that each match is a test.”

Having failed to win any of their first six league games, Fulham have now won back-to-back Premier League games, with consecutive 1-0 wins over Hull and Coventry, which has lifted them out of the relegation zone.

“It [managing in England] is a very tough challenge but I am so happy to be here,” Alvaro Arbeloa said. “I am where I want to be and I am really enjoying my days. I want to win games and I think we are performing well but we need to improve.

“They [Aston Villa] are very compact, they defend so well and even with the ball they know what they have to do. And they have top players, and when you have a top coach with top players, normally you have a top team. I think right now he [Unai Emery] is one of the best coaches in the world. He is very, very good, he improves everything every year. It does not matter where he is coaching, he is doing an amazing job, and for me also it is a very good challenge to face him.”

In the two league meetings between these sides last season, it was one win apiece; Aston Villa won this fixture 3-1 just over a year ago before Fulham won 1-0 at Craven Cottage back in April. Team news from Villa Park to follow shortly.

#994. West Ham were right to be ruthless with Nuno, but are they right about Scott Parker?

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Comment: Some feel it was harsh to sack Nuno now, but truthfully, he could have gone in the summer. The bigger question is whether his reported replacement is the right pick

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

“I am always under pressure, every day,” Nuno Espirito Santo said in the wake of Saturday’s 3-1 loss to West Brom. Not any more, he’s not.

An optimistic outlook on his removal as West Ham coach is that it offers respite. Respite from that pressure, which has never truly waned in his 13 months in charge. It might seem a ruthless move by the east London club to fire him “so early” into the season, but West Ham were right to be ruthless.

But let’s not forget that the Championship season is already a quarter of the way done, and true ruthlessness would have entailed sacking the Portuguese over the summer, after he failed to stop West Ham from plummeting into the Championship – despite taking over from Graham Potter in late September.

The former Nottingham Forest and Tottenham coach never truly steadied the ship in the Premier League. There was barely even a new-manager bounce to be buoyant about, never a moment when Hammers fans could breathe easily, and even the seas of the second tier (which he navigated so well by winning the league with Wolves in 2017/18) proved too choppy this time around.

That is not to say his West Ham side have been disastrous this season, but with immediate promotion essential from a financial standpoint – and in order to keep the best of this squad together – six wins, four draws, and three losses were never going to instil adequate confidence. Eighth place, one quarter of the way through the season, is too risky a spot.

It is OK to drop points intermittently in such a long, arduous campaign, but the move to sack Nuno was motivated by West Ham’s fear of those points practically spilling out underneath them, like marbles.

It would, of course, have been nice for fans to see a move not motivated by fear; perhaps a change in the summer would have felt harsh, but it would have been proactive, and there is an argument it would have felt encouraging in a different sense.

On the topic of encouragement, West Ham’s free-scoring start to the season was a refreshing sight after recent times at London Stadium, and they remain the highest-scoring team in the division, but their goal difference has already been matched.

And for Nuno, 52, and his players, the issue has not just been conceding too many goals, but also the timing of those errors: they have conceded first in nine out of their 16 games in all competitions. That has signalled a concerning fragility, which has tasked West Ham with fighting back far too often – in a season when many expected them to lead from the front, no less.

Admittedly, there was a degree of naivety to this sentiment. Over the summer, it was all too easy for neutral fans to assume that West Ham would walk the Championship, when supporters of the east London club knew how misguided these claims were. You need look no further than West Ham’s previous outing in the Championship, in 2011/12, when they let a top-two finish slip away before going life-and-death with Blackpool in the play-off final.

Again, that is far too risky a spot this time around, and cannot be justified when you own the most expensive squad in the league (at an estimated £282m, with the £18m gap to Wolves proving substantial at this level).

There is surely greater quality at West Ham than any other club in the Championship, and some observers will feel a coach would not need to get too much right to promote the Hammers. In that regard, Nuno was doing too much wrong.

With Scott Parker immediately emerging as the frontrunner to replace him, perhaps the conversation can move away from risk. But only in the short-term, you would think.

Parker, a former Hammer, secured promotion with Fulham, Bournemouth and Burnley in his first season in charge of each club. That record is remarkable. It is simply a shame the stories didn’t end there. Fulham and Burnley were immediately relegated in their subsequent seasons, while Parker left Bournemouth by the end of August after a shocking start to life in the Premier League.

Of course, as a West Ham fan, you might not care to look that far ahead. The priority is purely promotion to the Premier League.

Moreover, a feelgood factor could stem from the nostalgia of Parker’s return. To quote a great modern sketch by Exploding Heads: “He knows the club. He knows the ground... even though it’s different than when he was there.”

In all seriousness, there would be genuine appreciation towards the former midfielder, who won the fan-voted Hammer of the Year award three years in a row. Fans might hope fortunes have been hiding in plain sight.

“Mr West Ham” Mark Noble played alongside the 46-year-old at Upton Park and is now sporting director (he will oversee preparations for Wednesday’s game versus Cardiff). Would Noble and Parker have the chemistry in the office that they had on the pitch? Well, it’s worth noting that they were relegated together in 2011.

Against what you might assume, they would also be unlikely to settle the debate about the “West Ham Way” (chiefly, whether it even exists). While West Ham have scored an unusually high number of goals under Nuno this season, Parker’s MO is clean sheets; that would mark a jarring about-turn, stylistically.

But maybe an about-turn is what West Ham need. They are heading in the wrong direction, even if slowly, and slip-ups cannot be allowed to become a full-on skid. West Ham have problems higher up than in the managerial seat, but finding someone to fill it is the only immediate concern.

Newcastle United's reliance on the past is costing them dearly in the present after another home defeat

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The cruel irony of Newcastle United’s current predicament is that, for all they are looking to the future, they are too reliant on the past and it is costing them dearly in the present.

As the rain lashed down at St James’ Park on Monday night, it captured the sodden mood on Tyneside as Everton secured a third straight Premier League win on that famous ground courtesy of Thierno Barry’s second half goal.

Newcastle dropped to 13th in the table after a third defeat in four.

A sell out crowd greeted the final whistle with the sort of indignation which could be construed in a tipping point in their tolerance of the current state of affairs, something Matthias Jaissle insisted he understood as pressure on him grows.

"I was aware of the anger,” he told reporters afterwards. “Big frustration, big disappointment because we couldn't transfer what we saw in the week.

"The team was training at a high level, but since the ref started the game, not much was seen. It's difficult to understand. Of course the fans are frustrated, like we are.

"Unfortunately, we couldn't deliver. Actually, over the whole 90 minutes, it was not our game and our style of playing. That is something we are very frustrated and disappointed about. If you cannot deliver when it counts, then you don't deserve to win.”

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

With every passing game, it becomes clearer that the framing of the summer may have been wrong. Newcastle knew there would be huge transition, with the sales of Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali accounted for in advance.

The departures first of manager Eddie Howe and then captain Bruno Guimaraes just weeks out from the start of the Premier League season were not what the club wanted.

Yet, in an interview with TNT Sports before the 2-2 draw with Bournemouth on September 5, sporting director Ross Wilson insisted the summer had gone to plan “almost in its entirety”.

Out with the old and in with the new; a refresh, Newcastle 2.0. That is what the fans were told. After the success of the first five years under the Saudi Arabian Public Investment Fund, which yielded two Champions League campaigns and a trophy, Newcastle had hit their ceiling and it was necessary to take a step back to move forward again in a more sustainable manner.

Wilson spoke of giving youth a chance and taking risks - a fresh identity he hoped would help the club become more competitive in the long run. More than £200m was spent on eight new players, but the problem is Jaissle does not seem to count on a number of them.

Bazoumana Toure cost £42m, but the 20-year-old Ivorian has barely featured; the same can be said for £35m midfielder Aladji Bamba.

Following a stellar performance in the victory over Hull City on September 19, it was hoped Dutch teenager Sean Steur would be given more responsibility. His substitute appearance shortly after Barry’s opener was his first league appearance since.

The bold strategy set out has yet to come to fruition. It is hard to blame Jaissle for not having more trust, but the upshot is that Guimaraes’ replacement right now looks to be Joe Willock, a player who, it was almost universally felt for as long as a couple of years, had no future at Newcastle.

Replacing Alexander Isak’s goals, a year after his acrimonious departure for Liverpool, is the responsibility of Will Osula, his former understudy, despite £175m being spent on strikers since 2025.

Harvey Barnes, consistently used as a bit-part player while Gordon shone on the left, has been given his opportunity. At present, he simply isn’t taking it.

There are so many others, too. Jaissle brought Fabian Schar and Dan Burn back into the fold ahead of the victory over Crystal Palace last Sunday and it worked perfectly. Since returning from injury, too, Joelinton has been a regular in an unfamiliar deep midfield role, but his physicality and leadership are seen as too important to go without.

Newcastle rejected a £15m offer from Nottingham Forest for Jacob Murphy on transfer deadline day and he too has featured regularly this season.

All of these players were crucial in Newcastle’s recent success, but by complimenting the best players in the team. Now Isak, Guimaraes, Tonali and Gordon have left, making them more prominent naturally reduces the overall quality, and it is not hard to understand the sort of impact that has on progress.

Long-term, the hope is that Steur, Bamba and Toure will develop into players capable of filling the boots of the players who have gone. They certainly have the profile and potential to do so. But right now, there is a void in Newcastle's squad, an imbalance between its character and quality. Left unchecked, the consequences could be dire.
